care_summary: Bright indirect light. Let the top inch of soil dry between waterings, and water less in winter. Give it a moss pole or trellis: climbing helps it mature and produce split leaves, but light matters too.

Tolerates low to bright indirect light; no direct midday sun, and not a windowless room. Water when the top inch is dry, less in winter. Note: outdoors in tropical regions this species is invasive — never compost cuttings or release into the environment.

Tolerates low light and erratic watering, though it grows best in brighter indirect light. Let soil dry completely between waterings, and water less in winter; overwatering is the only common way to kill it.

citations.label: Kew Gardens — Plants of the World Online

care_summary: Bright indirect light. Water when the top inch dries, less in winter. Prolific producer of plantlets — clip and pot to share with friends.

Bright direct light, ideally a south- or west-facing window. Water deeply but only when soil is bone dry. Use a fast-draining cactus mix. The ASPCA lists it as toxic to cats and dogs, so keep it out of their reach.

citations.label: Iran J Med Sci — peer-reviewed review

care_summary: Low to medium light works; avoid direct sun. Likes evenly moist soil. Check the top inch. Water when it just starts to dry, before it droops, and less often in winter.

origin_note: Cultivar: Philodendron erubescens 'Pink Princess', a selection of a species native to Colombia.
care_summary: Cultivar selected for unstable pink variegation. Bright indirect light is non-negotiable — too little and the pink reverts to green. If the pink fades, prune back to a pink node and give brighter indirect light. Water when top inch is dry, less in winter. Stake to climb.
Collector species nicknamed the Queen Anthurium. Demands very high humidity (70%+), bright indirect light, and a chunky aroid mix. Not a beginner plant; water a little less in winter.
Stores water in rhizomes. Tolerates low light and missed waterings. Water only when soil is fully dry, and less in winter.
Glossy leaves love bright indirect light. Water when the top two inches of soil are dry, less in winter. Wipe leaves to keep them shining.
Wants a consistent spot in bright indirect light — hates being moved. Water when top two inches of soil are dry, less in winter. Sensitive to drafts.
Medium indirect light only — direct sun bleaches the silver bands. Keeps soil consistently moist, a little less in winter. Use filtered or rain water; tap water minerals burn the leaf edges.
Wants the brightest spot you can give it; flowers indoors only with several hours of direct sun. Water when the top two inches are dry; in winter, let the top few inches dry before watering.

citations.label: Kew Gardens — Plants of the World Online

care_summary: Native pollinator workhorse. Full sun and average garden soil. Water new plantings every few days for the first season; once established it is drought tolerant, so water only in long dry spells. Long-blooming for late-summer pollinators.

Native prairie perennial. Full sun and well-drained soil. Water new plantings every few days for the first season; once established it is drought tolerant, so water only in long dry spells. Leave the spent seed heads up over winter — finches feed on them.

Bright to medium indirect light indoors. Keep soil evenly moist. Outdoors in much of North America this species is aggressively invasive — never compost cuttings, and consider native alternatives like Virginia creeper (Parthenocissus quinquefolia).

origin_note: Cultivar: a David Austin English Rose bred in 2006 from garden rose hybrids, so it has no wild range.
care_summary: Famous David Austin cut-flower rose with peachy-apricot rosette blooms. A garden plant: full sun and well-drained soil. Check the soil and deep water about weekly in dry weather; a potted rose or tuber rots if watered on a short cycle. Disbud for fewer, bigger blooms — the standard florist trick.

citations.label: David Austin Roses — official cultivar page

care_summary: Cut-flower staple — round silvery juvenile leaves are the foliage you've seen in every wedding bouquet for a decade. Full sun, well-drained soil. Cut hard in spring to keep juvenile foliage.

native_range: Great Plains of the United States to Mexico
care_summary: Native to the southern Great Plains of the United States and Mexico; major commercial cut flower. Full sun, even moisture, neutral to alkaline soil. Long vase life (10–14 days) — handle stems gently, they bruise.

citations.label: Association of Specialty Cut Flower Growers

care_summary: Cool-season cut flower. Plant corms in fall where winters are mild, or in spring where they are cold; full sun and well-drained soil. Sappy stems — sear or hot-water dip after cutting for best vase life.
Bright indirect light. Let soil dry between waterings, and water less in winter. Don't deadhead spent flower spurs — Hoya re-flowers from the same peduncle for years.
Trailing succulent. Bright indirect light; soak, then let it dry fully. Pearls shrivel and flatten when dry. Translucent, mushy pearls mean overwatering.
Indirect light, high humidity, soil that never fully dries; water less often in winter. Browning fronds mean a dry root ball or dry air. Check the soil first.
Bright direct light keeps the leaves compact and red-edged. Water deeply only when soil is bone dry. A jade plant rarely outlives its owner — they get passed down generations.

native_range: Cultivar (parents in Dahlia pinnata lineage; native genus to Mexico)
origin_note: Cultivar: bred from the Dahlia pinnata lineage, whose wild ancestors are native to Mexico and Central America.
care_summary: The dinner-plate dahlia of wedding bouquets — blush, blooms 8–10 inches across. A garden plant: plant tubers after last frost in full sun and stake early. Check the soil and deep water about weekly in dry weather; potted tubers rot if watered on a short cycle. Lift tubers in cold-winter zones.

Bright, indirect light, such as an east or west window. Water about weekly in warm weather with tepid water and let it drain fully; the roots rot if they stay wet. Pot it in bark-based orchid mix, not regular potting soil, and keep it above 16°C.

Bright, indirect light; summer sun scorches the fronds. Keep the soil lightly moist but never waterlogged, and use rain or filtered water if your tap water is hard. It copes with cooler rooms, around 13°C in winter.

Filtered, medium light; direct sun burns the leaves. Keep the soil lightly moist and let the top dry a little between waterings. The ASPCA lists it as toxic to cats and dogs, so keep it away from pets.

Bright, indirect light with shade from hot sun. Water moderately while it is growing and sparingly in winter; let the top two inches dry between drinks. The ASPCA lists it as toxic to cats and dogs, so keep it out of reach.

native_range: Hybrid of two southeastern Brazilian rainforest species
origin_note: Hybrid of two southeastern Brazilian rainforest species, raised in cultivation. Often sold as Christmas cactus; many plants sold under that name are actually S. truncata (Thanksgiving cactus).
care_summary: A rainforest cactus, not a desert one. Bright, indirect light, away from strong sun, and potting mix that stays moist but never waterlogged. Two cool, drier rests (around 12 to 15°C), one in fall and one after flowering, help it set buds. Moving it or sudden temperature swings make the buds drop.

A small succulent that likes bright light but not hot midday sun. Use gritty cactus potting mix, water moderately while it grows, and keep it almost dry in winter. It rots if it sits in damp potting mix.

A rosette succulent that wants as much sun as you can give it, such as a south or west window. Use gritty, fast-draining potting mix. Water moderately while it grows and very little in winter, just enough to stop shrivelling. It rots if it stays wet.

A trailing succulent for bright, filtered light. Use gritty potting mix, water thoroughly, then let it dry out completely while it grows, and water sparingly in winter. The fat leaves drop off if it is knocked or moved a lot.

A slow plant that stores water in its swollen base, so it forgives forgotten waterings. Give it as much light as possible and water moderately while it grows, then keep it drier in winter. Overwatering is the way to lose it.

native_range: Central America and northern South America
care_summary: Bright light or partial shade, and potting mix that stays lightly moist but drains freely. Not the same plant as the jade plant, which is also sold as a money tree: check the Latin name on the label.

native_range: Origin uncertain; long cultivated in China and Japan
origin_note: Origin uncertain; long cultivated in China and Japan.
care_summary: Named for its toughness: it copes with low light, patchy watering and cool rooms (about 5 to 20°C). Keep it out of hot sun and away from heaters. The one way to harm it is soggy potting mix, which rots the roots.

native_range: Mexico, South America and the West Indies
care_summary: A compact, glossy plant that likes partial shade or filtered light and potting mix that is moist but well drained. Let the top of the potting mix dry a little between waterings. It is not related to the rubber plant (Ficus), which is a different species.

Bright light with some shade from hot sun. Water once the top 2 inches of potting mix is dry, and use rain or filtered water because fluoride in tap water browns the leaf tips. The ASPCA lists it as toxic to cats and dogs, so keep it out of reach.

Bright, filtered light. Water moderately while it grows and sparingly when it is resting, using gritty potting mix. The ASPCA lists it as toxic to cats and dogs, so keep it where pets cannot reach it.

A desert cactus that needs full sun and sharply draining potting mix. Water only once the potting mix has dried out while it grows, and keep it dry in winter. The ASPCA lists it as non-toxic to cats and dogs. The tiny barbed bristles and spines can still hurt, so handle it with folded newspaper.
